customers.name: Webshop Owner Running Their Own Warehouse
customers.description: Founder or co-owner of a Dutch or Belgian online store that has outgrown packing from spreadsheets and the webshop back-office. Ships roughly 25 to a few hundred orders a day from a small warehouse with a handful of (often part-time) staff, sells through one or more webshops and often bol. Picqer names about 25 orders a day as the point where it starts to help and positions itself as software you can set up yourself, "without consultants".
careAbout: Shipping every order on the day it was promised
Knowing true stock so the shop never oversells
Spending time on buying and marketing instead of firefighting in the warehouse
Predictable software cost that scales with orders
winsThem: Self-service setup in a day with store and carrier integrations that install in minutes
Purchase advice that tells them what to reorder per supplier
A 14-day free trial and unlimited free support
Peer cases from comparable webshops
theirFear: A long, consultant-driven WMS project that stalls the shop
Staff leaving and taking warehouse knowledge with them
Paying for an enterprise tool sized for a much larger operation
Integrations breaking during peak season

customerJourneyStories.name: From spreadsheets to a first WMS in a week
customerJourneyStories.summary: A growing webshop replaces Excel stock lists and a webshop plugin with Picqer.

stages.narrative: After a December in which items sold out online but were still on the shelf, and two temporary packers sent wrong products, the owner decides stock and picking must move out of spreadsheets.

He hears about Picqer from another webshop owner in an online entrepreneurs community, sees it in the Shopify app integrations and finds a Picqer warehouse-tips article when searching for how to organise locations.

He compares Picqer with a cheaper webshop WMS and the warehouse module of an ERP on price per order, ease of use and integrations, reads the pricing page (Team plan from 3,000 orders a month) and books a 30-minute demo.

During the 14-day trial he connects the webshop, bol and the carrier himself, labels locations on a Saturday and runs the warehouse on Picqer for a week with the support team answering questions in chat.
Every order now goes through scanning, the purchase advice is checked weekly and the first rules mark same-day orders as urgent.

As volume doubles, he adds users and a second label printer at no extra licence cost and moves to a larger plan; the full stock history and the team habits built on Picqer make switching unattractive.

customerJourneyStories.name: Outgrowing the ERP warehouse module
customerJourneyStories.summary: A wholesaler with a webshop moves warehouse execution from its ERP module to Picqer while the ERP stays the commercial system.

stages.narrative: After a peak season with late shipments and a growing gap between ERP stock and shelf stock, the operations director asks the warehouse manager for a real WMS that also supports handheld scanners.

The manager learns that Katapull, owner of the company's ERP vendor Logic4, has acquired Picqer and positions it as the next step for warehouse needs; he also knows Picqer from a logistics fair and peers.

He compares Picqer with an enterprise WMS and a fulfilment provider's WMS on batch picking, multi-warehouse, hardware support, API and price per order; he checks references and the status page history and asks how the ERP connection works.
A pilot runs one product group and the B2B portal on Picqer for four weeks, with orders and stock exchanged with the ERP through the API.
All orders move to Picqer; the team picks with Zebra handhelds, rules route heavy items to a dedicated zone and daily reports replace the whiteboard.
The company adds a conveyor and later a goods-to-person system through a Picqer hardware partner on the same system, and upgrades its plan as volume grows.

customerJourneyStories.name: Switching a fulfilment business to Picqer Fulfilment
customerJourneyStories.summary: A Dutch fulfilment company with about 40 clients replaces a rigid, increasingly expensive WMS.

stages.narrative: Each new client means a paid change request with the current WMS vendor, licence costs rise per client and the team spends three days a month on invoices.
The owner sees Picqer Fulfilment cases from other 3PLs, hears about it from webshop prospects who already use Picqer and visits Picqer at a fulfilment event.

She compares Picqer Fulfilment with a 3PL-specific WMS and an enterprise WMS on client separation, portal, configurability, price per order without per-client fees and batch traceability; a demo creates a trial account on the spot.
Three clients are migrated first: their webshops are connected, products imported and stock received while the rest stays on the old system for a month.
All clients run on one workflow; clients use the portal for stock and orders, comments with photos replace e-mails and packaging usage is recorded per shipment.
The company moves to Fulfilment Plus as it passes 400 orders a day, adopts batch and best-before tracking for a supplements client and waits for built-in client invoicing.

customerJourneyStories.name: Moving stock to a 3PL that runs Picqer
customerJourneyStories.summary: A supplements brand moves from its own garage warehouse to a fulfilment company and starts working in the portal.

stages.narrative: The founder can no longer pack orders herself and needs batch tracking demanded by a retailer.
Her shortlisted fulfilment company shows the Picqer Fulfilment portal in its sales pitch; she recognises Picqer from webshop forums.
She compares 3PLs partly on their software: real-time portal, Shopify connection, own carrier choice and batch tracking; she gets portal demo access.
The first delivery is received with batch numbers; she watches the first 100 orders flow through the portal and asks questions in comments.
She checks stock and slow movers weekly, creates B2B orders in the portal and uses purchase advice.
The transparency keeps her with the 3PL; when she opens a second sales channel it is connected in the same portal.

customerJourneyStories.name: A temp worker's first peak shift with the Picqer app
customerJourneyStories.summary: A student joins a webshop warehouse for the December peak.

stages.narrative: The webshop hires extra hands for peak and the student has never worked in a warehouse.
He first sees Picqer when the team lead hands him a handheld and a login; colleagues explain it in two minutes.
He decides whether he trusts the tool during his first batch: the route makes sense, the scanner beeps on wrong items.
On his first shift he picks batches alone after fifteen minutes and pauses one damaged item with a photo.
Within a week he uses singles picking, counts locations in quiet moments and answers comments in the app.
He returns the next peak and asks for the same tool; his feedback goes to the manager, who passes it to Picqer.

customerJourneyStories.name: A returns platform builds a native Picqer integration
customerJourneyStories.summary: A returns-management company (as Returnista did) connects to Picqer and becomes a Commerce Hub sibling.

stages.narrative: Several of the partner's webshop customers ask for returns to be pre-registered in their Picqer warehouse.
The partner finds Picqer's public API documentation and the partner page explaining how integrations come about.
It evaluates API coverage for orders, returns and webhooks, sandbox access and whether Picqer will list the integration.
A first version pre-registers returns for two shared customers; Picqer support helps test the scan-in flow.
The integration is listed on picqer.com and announced in a Picqer blog; shared customers grow.
Within Katapull, both companies plan tighter integration and joint offers, as Picqer's co-founder stated at the acquisition.
